vignette:
Mateo speaks of his life before as if describing a character in a novel he once read-a passionate, somewhat naive university student in his home country. He was studying political science, organizing student protests, and was in love with the idea of a better future. That life ended abruptly four years ago, in a windowless room with a concrete floor that was always damp. He doesn't offer details of the weeks he spent there, not in a linear way. The story comes in fragments, sensory snapshots that ambush him during the day. The sharp, chemical scent of bleach, the specific weight of a wet cloth over his face, the sound of a metal bucket scraping against the floor.

He eventually made his way to the United States, carrying a profound sense of disbelief that he was physically free. For the first year, adrenaline and the sheer novelty of survival propelled him forward. He met a woman, Elena, a kind soul who saw his quietness as strength. They married quickly, a desperate grasp at the normal life he felt he was supposed to be building. He found work cleaning houses-it required little English and allowed him to be anonymous, a ghost moving through other people's lives.

But the ghost of the concrete room was always with him. Elena would find him standing stock-still in their small apartment, staring at nothing, his hands clenched into fists. He couldn't sleep for more than an hour or two at a time before the nightmares ripped him awake, his own screams caught in his throat. He'd spend the rest of the night on the couch, watching the blue light of the television, convinced that if he relaxed, something terrible would happen. He stopped going to community gatherings; the sound of people speaking his native Spanish loudly felt like a threat, the laughter too sharp, too sudden.

His work became both a refuge and a minefield. The solitude was a comfort, but the triggers were everywhere. Last week, while scrubbing a client's gleaming white bathroom, the smell of the industrial-strength cleaner sent him reeling. For a moment, he was no longer in a suburban home, but back on that cold floor, the air thick with the smell of his own fear and disinfectant. He had to brace himself against the sink, his knuckles white, and breathe through his mouth until the tiled walls stopped closing in. Another time, a client came home early, the unexpected sound of a key in the lock sending a jolt of pure terror through him. He dropped a glass, and his first instinct was to hide, to make himself small in the corner of the kitchen.

The marriage to Elena crumbled under the weight of the man he had become. He couldn't explain the chasm that had opened inside him. Touch felt like a violation, intimacy an impossibility. He saw the confusion and hurt in her eyes as he flinched away from her hand on his shoulder. He was incapable of joy, and his numbness was a poison that leached the color from her own life. When she left, he felt a flicker of something-not sadness, but a grim confirmation of a belief that had taken root in that room: he was ruined, unclean, and destined to be alone.

Now, at 26, his world has shrunk to the houses on his route. He is meticulous, scrubbing away dirt that only he can see. He finds a temporary, fragile peace in bringing order to other people's chaos. But when the work is done, he returns to his empty apartment. He sits in the dark, tracing the patterns on the linoleum with his eyes, waiting for the sun to rise, always waiting, forever on guard.
